nodes.name: Basic properties of the adapted complex structure (Grauert tube)
nodes.statement: Among the compatible properties of the tube structure is that the length-squared function $\tau = \|v\|^2, v \in TM$ is a strictly plurisubharmonic function on the tube, and its square root $u =\sqrt{\tau}$ is a solution of the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation (HCMA) on the complement of the zero section, whose associated characteristic foliation is the geodesic foliation, or Riemann foliation, in $TM$.
nodes.statement_short: On the tube, $\tau=\|v\|^2$ is strictly plurisubharmonic and $u=\sqrt{\tau}$ solves the HCMA with the Riemann foliation as characteristic foliation.
conclusions: the length-squared function $\tau = \|v\|^2, v \in TM$ is a strictly plurisubharmonic function on the tube
its square root $u =\sqrt{\tau}$ is a solution of the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation (HCMA) on the complement of the zero section

nodes.name: Lempert-Szőke curvature condition
nodes.statement: Lempert and Sz\H{o}ke \cite{ls} have shown that a necessary condition for the tube of $(M, g)$ to be entire is that the sectional curvatures of $g$ be non-negative.
nodes.statement_short: If the Grauert tube of $(M,g)$ is entire then $g$ has non-negative sectional curvature.
assumptions: the tube of $(M, g)$ to be entire
conclusions: the sectional curvatures of $g$ be non-negative

nodes.name: Szőke's classification of entire tubes for metrics of revolution on $S^2$
nodes.statement: Sz\H{o}ke has shown that there is only a two parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$ which have entire tubes, whereas many of these manifolds have strictly positive curvature.
assumptions: metrics of revolution on $S^2$
conclusions: there is only a two parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$ which have entire tubes

nodes.name: Aguilar's higher order conditions for entire tubes
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $M$ of two dimensions, Aguilar \cite{a2} has found an infinite sequence of conditions generalizing that of Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke to higher order invariants which give necessary and sufficient conditions that a tube be entire.
nodes.statement_short: For surfaces, an infinite sequence of higher-order invariants gives necessary and sufficient conditions for an entire tube.
assumptions: for $M$ of two dimensions
conclusions: an infinite sequence of conditions generalizing that of Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke to higher order invariants which give necessary and sufficient conditions that a tube be entire

nodes.name: Effective finiteness of Aguilar's conditions
nodes.statement: In particular, it is not known whether the conditions are effectively finite, i.e., are redundant after a certain degree.

nodes.name: Szőke's theorem: bi-invariant metrics have entire tubes
nodes.statement: If the metric $g$ is bi-invariant on $G$, then Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s} has shown that the tube is entire and equal to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$.
assumptions: the metric $g$ is bi-invariant on $G$
conclusions: the tube is entire and equal to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$

nodes.name: Some left-invariant metrics on $SU(2)$ have no entire tube
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is well-known that some left-invariant metrics on $S^3 = SU(2)$ have scalar curvature $R < 0$, which shows they cannot have entire tubes, by Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke's condition.
assumptions: some left-invariant metrics on $S^3 = SU(2)$ have scalar curvature $R < 0$
conclusions: they cannot have entire tubes

nodes.name: Arnol'd's rigid body correspondence
nodes.statement: It is a well-known observation of Arnol'd that the geodesic flow for a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group is equivalent to the motion of a free rigid body whose frame is parametrized by $G$ about its center of mass (see \cite{via}, Appendix 2, for example).
nodes.origin_citation: Arnol'd 1978 (Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, App. 2)
nodes.statement_short: Geodesic flow of a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group = motion of a free rigid body with frame in $G$.
assumptions: a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group
conclusions: is equivalent to the motion of a free rigid body whose frame is parametrized by $G$ about its center of mass

nodes.name: Entire tube of a homogeneous space is $G_{\mathbb{C}}/H_{\mathbb{C}}$
nodes.statement: In particular, if $G$ acts transitively on $M$, with isotropy group $H$ at a reference point $z_0 \in M$, then the entire Grauert tube is biholomorphic to $G_{\mathbb{C}}/H_{\mathbb{C}}.$
assumptions: $G$ acts transitively on $M$, with isotropy group $H$ at a reference point $z_0 \in M$
conclusions: the entire Grauert tube is biholomorphic to $G_{\mathbb{C}}/H_{\mathbb{C}}.$

nodes.name: Generic left-invariant metrics on $SU(2)$ do not have entire tubes
nodes.statement: For a generic left-invariant metric one can show, using the mechanical integrals of motion, that the map $Exp_{\mathbb{C}}$ is not well-defined on all of $i TG$ because most complexified (real) geodesics are not given by entire functions into $G_{\mathbb{C}}$.
nodes.statement_short: For generic (pairwise distinct eigenvalue) left-invariant metrics, $Exp_{\mathbb{C}}$ is not defined on all of $iTG$: complexified geodesics are not entire.
assumptions: a generic left-invariant metric
conclusions: the map $Exp_{\mathbb{C}}$ is not well-defined on all of $i TG$

nodes.name: canonical one-form $\Theta$
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi: TM \to M$ denote the projection, and let $\Theta$ denote the canonical one-form on $TM$ given by 

\[
	\Theta(V) := (D\pi(V), v),
\]

where $v \in T_{\pi(v)}M, V \in T_v(TM)$, and $(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the Riemannian metric $g$.

nodes.name: adapted complex structure
nodes.statement: An {\em adapted complex structure} on $T^RM := \{v \in TM \, | \, |v| < R\}$ is a complex structure for which the leaves of the Riemann foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $TM \setminus 0_M$ are complex submanifolds.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
differentia: the leaves of the Riemann foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $TM \setminus 0_M$ are complex submanifolds

nodes.name: Grauert tube
nodes.statement: For the maximal radius $R$ for which the adapted complex structure is defined, the complex manifold $T^RM$ is called the {\em Grauert tube} of $(M, g)$.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: entire tube
nodes.statement: If $R = +\infty$, we say the tube is {\em entire}.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Isometries act holomorphically on the Grauert tube (property (1))
nodes.statement: If $\phi$ is an isometry of $(M, g)$, then its action by its differential $D\phi$ on the Grauert tube $T^RM$ is holomorphic for the adapted complex structure, while the map $v \to -v$ is anti-holomorphic.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
assumptions: $\phi$ is an isometry of $(M, g)$
conclusions: its action by its differential $D\phi$ on the Grauert tube $T^RM$ is holomorphic for the adapted complex structure
the map $v \to -v$ is anti-holomorphic

nodes.name: Strict plurisubharmonicity of $r^2$ (property (2))
nodes.statement: The function $r^2 := |v|^2$ given by the $g$-length squared of vectors is strictly plurisubharmonic on the tube.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
conclusions: The function $r^2 := |v|^2$ given by the $g$-length squared of vectors is strictly plurisubharmonic on the tube.

nodes.name: Liouville form is Kähler (property (3))
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
nodes.statement_short: $\frac i2\partial\bar\partial r^2$ equals the Liouville form $d\Theta$, which is Kähler and induces $g$ on the zero section.
conclusions: is the Liouville form on $TM$ and is a K\"ahler form
The corresponding K\"ahler metric induces the original metric $g$ along the zero section $M$.

nodes.name: Liouville form identity
nodes.statement: \frac{i}2 \partial \bar{\partial} r^2 = d\Theta := \Omega
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: $r$ solves the homogeneous complex Monge-Ampère equation (property (4))
nodes.statement: $r$ satisfies the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation $\partial \bar{\partial} u^n = 0$ on $T^RM \setminus M$.

conclusions: $r$ satisfies the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation $\partial \bar{\partial} u^n = 0$ on $T^RM \setminus M$.

nodes.name: $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}$ is a holomorphic vectorfield on the tube

It follows from the property (1) above for Grauert tubes that $\Phi^{\tilde{\xi}}_t$ acts biholomorphically on the tube, and thus

nodes.name: Szőke's theorem on holomorphic $G_{\mathbb{C}}$-action on entire tubes
nodes.statement: Let $(M, g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold with entire Grauert tube. Then the complex group $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts holomorphically on all of the tube, i.e., on all of $TM$ with the adapted complex structure.

nodes.name: Entire tube of a left-invariant metric is $G_{\mathbb{C}}$

Then the 	connected complex group $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts simply transitively on $M_{\mathbb{C}} := TM$, i.e., the entire tube $TM$ is biholomorphic to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement:
By lemma \ref{lemma:action}, we know that $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$. We will prove that it acts locally transitively at every point $v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$. Assuming this for the moment, this proves that all orbits of $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are open, and since $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ is connected, this proves that the mapping $A_v: G_{\mathbb{C}} \ni h \to h\cdot v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$, for any fixed $v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$, is surjective. Since $G_{\mathbb{C}}, M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are of the same complex dimension, and the map $A_v$ is $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ equivariant, Sard's theorem says that every point in $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ is a regular value of $A_v$, and hence, $A_v$ is a topological covering. If $v \in M$, the covering $A_v: G \to M$ is a diffeomorphism. Since the inclusions $G \subset G_{\mathbb{C}}, M \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are homotopy equivalences, the covering $A_v$ has degree 1 over all of $M_{\mathbb{C}}$, and therefore $A_v$ is a global biholomorphism.
\vskip 2mm
\vskip 2mm
To show that $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts locally transitively, it suffices to show that 

\[
	DA_{v}: T^{1,0}_{I} G_{\mathbb{C}} = \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} \to T_v^{1,0} M_{\mathbb{C}}
\]

is an isomorphism. This, in turn is equivalent to showing that, for a basis $\xi_1, \xi_2,\ldots, \xi_n$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ over $\mathbb{R}$, the complex fields $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2, \ldots, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n$ are a basis for $T^{1,0}M_{\mathbb{C}}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ at $v$. Define $\mathcal{P} = \{ \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1 \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2 \wedge \ldots \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n = 0\}$. We wish to show $\mathcal{P}$ is empty. 

\vskip 2mm

Assume it is not empty. Then $\mathcal{P}$ is a $G_{\mathbb{C}}$-invariant divisor on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$, and $\mathcal{P} \cap M = \emptyset$. Consider the plurisubharmonic function $u$ restricted to $\mathcal{P}$. Since $u$ is non-negative and proper when restricted to $\mathcal{P}$, it achieves a global minimum at some $v \in \mathcal{P}$. The map $A_v$ restricted to $G$ gives an embedding of $G$ into $\mathcal{P} \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$ where it is a $CR$-submanifold of real dimension $n$. Note that the function $u$ is constant on $S_v := A_v(G)$. Since $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} \mathcal{P} < n$, $S_v$ cannot be a totally real submanifold in $\mathcal{P}$. Hence its complex tangent space is positive dimensional at every point. Its Levi-form cannot be trivial, since otherwise the leaves of the Levi foliation of $S_v$ would give positive-dimensional complex submanifolds in the level set $\{u = u(v)\}$, which is strictly pseudoconvex, by the tube construction. By a classical construction in complex analysis (local Bishop disks), there exists a continuous mapping $F: \bar{\triangle} \to U \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$, where $U$ is a small polydisk neighborhood of $v$, and with $F|_{\triangle}$ holomorphic and non-constant, and $F(\partial \triangle) \subset S_v$. Thus $u\circ F|_{\partial\triangle} \equiv u(v)$. Therefore, $F(\triangle) \subset \mathcal{P} \cap U$, since $\mathcal{P} \cap U$ is closed and analytic in $U$, which gives us that $u\circ F(z) \geq u(v),$ for all $z \in \triangle$. By the maximum principle, $u\circ F$ is constant on $\triangle$, contradicting, again, the strict pseudoconvexity of $S_v$.

nodes.name: Argument for Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: This map is, at first, just defined in a neighborhood of the zero section $G$. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2

\[
	B = \left(\begin{array}{cccc} \lambda_1 z_1 & \lambda_2 \, z_2 & \lambda_3 \, z_3 & - a \, w \\	& & & \\ \lambda_1^2 \, z_1 & \lambda_2^2 \, z_2 & \lambda_3^2 \, z_3 & - b \, w \end{array} \right).
\]  


We wish to show that there are no $(z_1, z_2, z_3, w) \neq (0,0,0,0)$ which solve (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:qm}), and for which the rank of $B$ is $<$ 2, or the six $2\times 2$ minors of $B$ are 0:

\[
\begin{array}{rcl} 
	0 & = & \lambda_1 \, \lambda_2 (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) \, z_1 \, z_2 \\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_1 \, \lambda_3 \,(\lambda_3 - \lambda_1)\, z_1\, z_3 \\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_2 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_2)\, z_2 \, z_3 \\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_1\, (b - \lambda_1 \, a) \, z_1 \, w\\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_2 \, (b - \lambda_2 \, a) \, z_2 \, w \\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_3 \, (b - \lambda_3 \, a) \, z_3 \, w.
\end{array}
\]

On the other hand, it is clear that any 4-tuple $(z_1, z_2, z_3, w)$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:qe}) or (\ref{eqn:qm}) must have at least two non-zero components, while on the other hand, all the constants in this last array of equations are non-zero under our assumptions. This is a contradiction, hence $C_{a,b}$ is smooth.

\[

where $K_{\mathcal{Q}_{E,a}}$ is the canonical class of $\mathcal{Q}_{E,a} \sim -2 H$, where $H$ in turn is the hyperplane section of $\mathcal{Q}_{E,a} \subset \mathbb{P}^3$. Since $C_{a,b} \sim 2 H$, we see that $g(C) = 1$, as claimed.

But this last intersection is non-empty and a holomorphic map of $\mathbb{C}$ to $C^{aff}_{a,b}$ must factor through the universal covering $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to C_{a,b}$, but must omit the infinite set $\pi^{-1}(C_{a,b} \cap\{w = 0\})$. Thus, the map $c$ must be constant, by Picard's theorem. In real terms, this means that the real geodesic satisfies

\[
	\dot{\gamma} \equiv \xi \in \mathfrak{g},
\]

If we assume, without loss of generality, that $\gamma(0) = e \in G,$ this means that $\gamma(s)$ is the 1-parameter subgroup $\exp(s \xi)$ of $G$. Now this conclusion holds true for all initial conditions $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_0$ in a dense open set of $\mathfrak{g} = T_0G.$ By continuity of solution of ODEs, this must hold true for all geodesics passing through 0, and hence, by left translation, for all geodesics. However, it is well-known that any left invariant metric for which all geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups is necessarily bi-invariant and hence round (see e.g. \cite{o}, ch. 11, Proposition 9). This would contradict our assumption that the $\lambda_i$ are all distinct.

nodes.name: Why the Picard argument fails when $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$
nodes.statement:
To be specific, we set $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, the other case being similar. In this case, equations (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:qm}) can be reduced to the pair of equations (\ref{eqn:qe}) and

\begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} 0 & = & (\lambda_1 \lambda_3 - \lambda_3^2) \, z_3^2 - (\lambda_1 \, a - b) \, w^2 \\
					& & \\
					& = & \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_1 - \lambda_3) \, ( z_3^2 - \frac{\lambda_1 \, a - b}{\lambda_3 \, (\lambda_1 - \lambda_3)} \, w^2)
	\end{array}
\end{equation}

Using our notation for the initial condition $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_0 = x_1^o \, \xi_1 + x_2^o \, \xi_2 + x_3^o \, \xi_3,$ we can express

\[
	a = E(x^o), b = M(x^o),
\]

from which we can solve for 

\[
	\frac{\lambda_1 \, a - b}{\lambda_3 \, (\lambda_1 - \lambda_3)} = (x_3^o)^2.
\]	

It follows that (\ref{eqn:split}) splits over $\mathbb{R}$ and the curve defined by (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:split}) is the union of two curves

\[
	C^+_{a,b} = \mathcal{Q}_{E,a} \cap \{ z_3 = x_3^o \, w\} 
\]

and

\[	
	C^-_{a,b} = \mathcal{Q}_{E,a} \cap \{z_3 = - x_3^o \, w\}. 
\]

Each of these curves is a conic $\mathbb{P}^1 \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ which intersects the plane at infinity $\{w = 0\}$ in two points generically, so $C^{\text{aff}, \pm}_{a,b}$ is generically biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^*$, which certainly contains the images of non-trivial entire mappings from $\mathbb{C}$. Thus the method of proof for the case of $\lambda_i$ pairwise distinct will not work here. In fact, if $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$ then the tube of the metric $g_A$ is sometimes entire.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement:
This is an immediate consequence of a result of Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s2} (cf also \cite{a1}). The metric (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) has an isometry group $G \times S^1$ where the factor $S^1$ acts by right multiplication on $G$ by the 1-parameter subgroup $e^{t\, \xi_3}$ on the right, i.e., by $R_{e^{t\, \xi_3}}$, periodic of period $2\pi$, and the factor $G$ acts by left multiplication $L_g$ on $G$. Consider the manifold $G \times S^1$, where $G$ is given the bi-invariant metric of sectional curvature 1, which is the special case of (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda_1= 1$, and the $S^1$ factor is given the metric $\mu d\theta^2,$ where $d\theta^2$ is the invariant metric of length $2\pi$ on $S^1$ and $\mu$ is a real constant $> 0$. So $G\times S^1$ has the metric $g_{\mu}$ defined by

\begin{equation} g_{\mu} = g_I \oplus \mu \, d\theta^2.
\end{equation}


Consider the quotient manifold of $G\times S^1$ by the action of $S^1 = \{e^{i t}\}$ on $G\times S^1$ given by $e^{i t} \cdot (g, e^{i \theta}) = (g\cdot e^{2 t\, \xi_3}, e^{i(\theta + t)}).$ Then it is easy to see that the quotient manifold $G\times S^1/\sim$ is diffeomorphic to $G$. Let $\bar{g}_{\mu}$ be the Riemannian submersion metric from (\ref{eqn:gmu}). By construction, this metric is invariant under left translation by $G$ and by right translation by $e^{- t \, \xi_3}$. Consequently, it is one of the left invariant metrics on  $G$ with an extra isometric action from the right. It is an easy calculation to see which ones arise in this manner. Let 

\begin{equation} A = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & & \\ & 1 & \\ & & \lambda \end{array}\right).
\end{equation}

Explicitly, we will normalize our metrics so that $g_A(\xi_1, \xi_1) = g_A(\xi_2, \xi_2) = \frac14,$ and $g_A(\xi_3, \xi_3) = \frac{\lambda}4$.\footnote{This means that instead of $g_A(\cdot,\cdot) = -B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$, we now have $g_A(\cdot, \cdot) = -\frac18 B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$.} With this normalization, the case $A = I$ gives the round metric with sectional curvature $K = 1$ on $G \cong S^3$.
\vskip 2mm

We want to see which $\lambda$ in (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) will arise from Sz\H{o}ke's construction. Computing at $(e,1) \in G\times S^1$, the tangent vector to the $S^1$ action we will quotient by is given by $(2\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta})$. The projection of $(\xi_3, 0)$ onto this direction is given by

\begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl}
	(\xi_3,0)^T & = & \frac{((\xi_3, 0), (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}))}{|\xi_3 + \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}|^2} (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}), \\
	& & \\
	& = & \frac2{2+\mu} (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta})
	\end{array}
	
\end{equation}

and hence the normal component is given by 

\begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl}
		(\xi_3,0)^N & = & (\xi_3,0) - (\xi_3,0)^T \\
		&	&	\\
		& = & (\frac{\mu}{2+\mu} \xi_3, \frac2{2+\mu} \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}). 	
	\end{array}
	
\end{equation}

Thus, 

\[
	|\xi_3^N|^2 = 2 \frac{\mu}{2+\mu},
\]

which means that the quotient metric on $G$ is $g_A$ with $A$ in (\ref{eqn:A}) having $\lambda = \frac{\mu}{2 + \mu}.$ Hence, any $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ appears. The limit case $\mu = +\infty$ is just the case of the round sphere, $\lambda = 1$, which also has an entire tube, of course.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be the real geodesic on $G$ with initial conditions $\gamma(0) = e \in G$ and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = v_0 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$. We solve the geodesic equations (\ref{eqn:geodeqns1}) in the appendix \cite{web} relatively explicitly to show that the complexified geodesic $\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}(\zeta)$ is an entire function from $\mathbb{C}$ to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$. The other statements in the proposition follow from smooth dependence on initial conditions.
\vskip 2mm
For convenience, we repeat here the equations (\ref{eqn:geodeqns1}) from \cite{web} for the tangent vector $T = a\, \xi_1+b\, \xi_2+c\, \xi_3$ to a geodesic, subject to the initial condition $T(0) = a_0 \, \xi_1+ b_0\, \xi_2 +c_0 \, \xi_3,$ for a metric of the form $g_A$,  with $A$ as in (\ref{eqn:A}):
\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		\dot{a} & = & -b\, c\, (\lambda - 1) \\
		&&\\
		\dot{b} & = & - a\, c\, (1 - \lambda) \\
		&&\\
		\dot{c} & = & 0,
	\end{array}
\]


where $\dot{a} = T(a)$, etc. We get that $c \equiv c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and the system reduces to 


\[
	\begin{array}{rcr}
		\dot{a} & = & -\nu\, b \\
		&&\\
		\dot{b} & = & \nu \, a, 
	\end{array}
\]


with $\nu = c_0 \, (\lambda - 1) \in \mathbb{R}$. Hence, 

\vskip 2mm

\[
	\begin{array}{rcl} a & \equiv & a_0 \cos \nu \, t - b_0 \sin \nu \,t \\&&\\ b & \equiv & b_0 \cos \nu \,t + a_0 \sin \nu \, t, \end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm
where $t$ is the parameter of integration in the equations. Set 

\[
	T_{\mathbb{C}} = a(\zeta) \, \xi_{1,\mathbb{C}} +b(\zeta) \, \xi_{2,\mathbb{C}} + c_0 \, \xi_{3,\mathbb{C}},
\] 

which is an entire function from $\mathbb{C} \to \mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C}) \subset \mathbb{C}^4.$ Considering $\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}$ as a function from, at first, a neighborhood of $\mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}$ to $G_{\mathbb{C}} = SL(2,\mathbb{C}) \subset \mathbb{C}^4$, we have that it satisfies the equation 

\[
	\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}(\zeta)^{-1} \cdot \dot{\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}} = T_{\mathbb{C}},
\]

where $\dot{\gamma}_{\mathbb{C}} = \frac{d\;\;}{d \zeta}$, since we are using the left-invariant parallelism to trivialize $T^{1,0}G_{\mathbb{C}}$. Equivalently, we have

\[
	  \dot{\gamma}_{\mathbb{C}} = \gamma_{\mathbb{C}} \cdot T_{\mathbb{C}},
	 \]
	 
which is a linear equation, with $T_{\mathbb{C}}$ entire and known, on all of $\mathbb{C}$. Hence all its solutions extend to entire functions, proving the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the geodesic equations explicitly (velocity rotates with frequency $\nu$), so $T_{\mathbb{C}}$ is entire and $\dot\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}=\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}T_{\mathbb{C}}$ is a linear ODE with entire solutions.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.3
nodes.statement:
By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to \vskip 2mm
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		
		\item Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		
		\item Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vskip 2mm 
			\begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right).
			\end{equation}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		\item Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		
		\item Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$.
	\end{enumerate}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm

We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition.

\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm

Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}):
	
	\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\mathbb{H} & = &  b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, 
	\end{array}
	\]

where $a, b, c ,d \in \mathbb{R}$. (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say

\vskip 2mm

\[
\begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\mathbb{H}'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm
and

\vskip 2mm

	\[
	\begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array}
	\]
	
	\vskip 2mm
Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have

\vskip 2mm

\begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\  \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right).
\end{equation}


\vskip 2mm


As to step (3), as  in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly:

\vskip 2mm

\[
	\begin{array}{rcccl}
		\eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\
			&&&&\\
		\eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3.
	\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm

so that we have 


\vskip 2mm


\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		\left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot  \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\  \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\
		& = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin  t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). 
	\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm

It follows directly that

\vskip 2mm

\[ 
	Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right).
\]

\vskip 2mm

Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if 

\vskip 2mm

\begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t.
\end{equation}

\vskip 2mm

It is clear pictorially or from an elementary calculus computation that, if $\lambda >1$, there is a unique $t_*(\lambda) > 0$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:tstar}), as claimed
nodes.statement_short: Solve the Jacobi equation along $\exp(t\xi_1)$, change to the right-invariant frame, and apply the rank formula of Lemma 3.3; singularity iff $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$, which has a unique positive root.

nodes.name: Four-step plan
nodes.statement:
By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to \vskip 2mm
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		
		\item Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		
		\item Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vskip 2mm 
			\begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right).
			\end{equation}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		\item Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		
		\item Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$.
	\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.3, singularities are zeros of $\Delta(t)$ obtained in four steps

nodes.name: Item (1)
nodes.statement: Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the Jacobi equation along $\exp(t\xi_1)$

nodes.name: Item (2)
nodes.statement_short: Impose initial conditions (5.6)

nodes.name: Item (3)
nodes.statement: Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$
nodes.statement_short: Change to the right-invariant frame

nodes.name: Item (4)
nodes.statement: Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate and solve $\Delta(t)=0$

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a unique positive root of $\Delta$

nodes.name: Step (1)-(2): Jacobi fields
nodes.statement:
Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}):
	
	\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\mathbb{H} & = &  b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, 
	\end{array}
	\]

where $a, b, c ,d \in \mathbb{R}$. (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say

\vskip 2mm

\[
\begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\mathbb{H}'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm
and

\vskip 2mm

	\[
	\begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array}
	\]
	
	\vskip 2mm
Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have

\vskip 2mm

\begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\  \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use the appendix solution (7.21) and initial conditions to get (5.7)

nodes.name: Step (3): change of frame
nodes.statement:
As to step (3), as  in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly:

\vskip 2mm

\[
	\begin{array}{rcccl}
		\eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\
			&&&&\\
		\eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3.
	\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm

so that we have 


\vskip 2mm


\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		\left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot  \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\  \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\
		& = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin  t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). 
	\end{array}
\]
nodes.statement_short: Rotate by $Ad(\exp(-t\xi_1))$ to get $\alpha_i,\beta_i$

nodes.name: Step (4): imaginary part and $\Delta$
nodes.statement:
It follows directly that

\vskip 2mm

\[ 
	Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right).
\]

\vskip 2mm

Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if 

\vskip 2mm

\begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At imaginary time the matrix is diagonal; $\Delta=0$ iff (5.8)

nodes.statement: Can one carry out such a study as here for groups other than $SU(2)$?

nodes.name: Exact finite radius of tubes for $\lambda>1$
nodes.statement: It may also be possible to determine the finite radius of the tubes for $\lambda \in (1,+\infty)$ using the explicit solution for the tangent vector along a geodesic for such geometries, as in section \ref{sec:U2cases} above.

nodes.name: Tube radius estimates via Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick
nodes.statement: One might also find an estimate for the tube radius using an approximation to the constant negative curvature metrics on the affine elliptic curves given by the complex integrals of motion and the Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick inequality. It is unclear how such bounds would compare to the Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke curvature bound when both bounds apply.

nodes.name: Entire tubes on non-normal homogeneous spaces
nodes.statement: Finally, can anything interesting be said of the case of a compact Riemannian homogeneous space $G/H$ which is not normal, i.e., not the Riemannian quotient of a symmetric metric on $G$?

nodes.name: Gelfand-Cetlin quantum integrable systems on flag manifolds
nodes.statement: A related question would be whether Gelfand-Cetlin quantum integrable systems exist on flag manifolds, which contain the Laplacian for a non-normal homogeneous metric.

nodes.name: Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}$
nodes.statement:
In general, if $\gamma$ is a Riemannian geodesic with $\dot{\gamma} := T$, so that $\nabla_T T = 0$, the Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}$ associates to a vectorfield $Y$ along $\gamma$ and normal to $\gamma$ the normal field along $\gamma$ given by

\[
	\mathcal{J}(Y) := \nabla_T^2 Y + Riem(Y, T) T.
\]
